Here is the breakdown of exactly how to optimize the "Rattle-Nut" for a 250 Hz acoustic vibration.

1. Clearance / Tolerance (The Most Important Variable)

For vibratory creep to occur, the nut must physically be able to bounce side-to-side (radially) against the rod. This is called "transverse vibration."

If the nut fits tightly on the threads, it will simply absorb the 250 Hz energy and act as a dampener. It must be intentionally sloppy.

  • The Optimization: When prototyping this on the Bambu Lab A1, you want to design a massive tolerance gap between the internal threads of the nut and the external threads of the rod. You are aiming for a loose, rattling fit—usually a clearance of at least 0.2 mm to 0.4 mm. Every time the 250 Hz hum hits, that loose clearance allows the thread flanks to separate for a microsecond, eliminating static friction and allowing gravity to pull it down a fraction of a millimeter.

2. Surface Finish vs. Lubricant

You actually do not want to use a liquid lubricant like oil or grease. Viscous fluids act as shock absorbers; they will soak up the microscopic 250 Hz acoustic energy and stop the nut from rattling entirely.

  • Fine Threads (Shallow Angle): A standard machine-screw thread pitch means the nut has to rotate many more times to travel the same vertical distance. A shallow pitch requires sustained, multi-day vibration to finally unscrew the nut all the way to the bottom.

Thick "Auger" Threads

When you picture an auger, you are likely picturing a thread with a very steep angle (high pitch) and a deep, thick profile (like an ACME or square thread).

Thin "Bolt" Threads

Standard, fine machine-screw threads have a very shallow angle and typically use a 60-degree V-shape profile.

  • The Angle (Flat Hill): A fine thread acts like a very shallow ramp. The vast majority of gravity's force is directed straight into the rod, not down the slope. It requires significant, prolonged vibratory energy to cause the nut to rotate even a fraction of a degree.
  • The Delay Time: Very long. This is how you achieve a multi-day timer. The nut has to rotate hundreds or thousands of times to travel a single inch.

Graphite would help immensely, and it is arguably the single best lubricant for this specific acoustic application.

Here is exactly why it outperforms other options in this scenario:

  • It Doesn't Dampen: As discussed, liquid lubricants (oils, greases) are viscous. If you put oil in the thread gap, the fluid will act exactly like a shock absorber, soaking up the microscopic 250 Hz acoustic waves before they can bounce the nut. Graphite is a dry solid, so it maintains the rigid, hard-surface contact necessary to transfer the acoustic vibration from the rod to the nut.
  • It Fills the Micro-Pores: 3D printed parts have microscopic layer lines and porous surfaces, which create high static friction. When you rub graphite powder into the plastic, the microscopic flakes fill those layer lines, turning a textured printed surface into a glassy, slick plane.
  • Shear Planes: Graphite works because its molecular structure looks like a deck of playing cards. When compressed between the nut and the rod, those "cards" slide effortlessly across one another. It reduces the static friction coefficient to near zero without adding any sticky residue.

If you use graphite, you can use a much lighter nut and a much shallower thread pitch, which gives you far more granular control over exactly how many days the timer will run.

If you secure the nut to the trap wall and let the bolt slowly vibrate its way downward, the physical properties of the mechanism change as it drops.

The Advantage of a Falling Nut

By rigidly securing the threaded rod to the hive wall, the rod becomes a permanent, unchanging extension of the wooden box. It transfers the 250 Hz vibration equally and consistently across its entire length.

Because the nut is the only thing moving, the tuning never changes. The nut will experience the exact same vibratory energy at the top of the threads as it does at the bottom.
